payload.text:
**The Cartographer of Small Hours**

I.

There is a country no map has ever met,
bounded by coffee rings and cold tea,
where the only roads are the ones you walk
before the kettle wakes — and back again,
when the kettle wakes, and the light
has moved an inch, and the room
is no longer the room that let you sleep in it.

II.

My grandmother kept time by the creaks
in the floor: the third step after the door,
the one that sang like a wire about to snap,
the one that swallowed sound. She knew
the house the way you know a hand —
by pressure, not by name. When the floors
settled in the cold, she said the house
was remembering something it had carried,
and she left the back door open an inch
so the memory could get out.

III.

You will grow old in a language
you never fully learned.
Every word you trust will lie to you once —
"forever," first of all, that little liar
who weighs nothing in the mouth
and everything in the chest.
"Young" is a word that only works
if you turn it around.

IV.

Somewhere a river is practicing a bend
it will wear into the stone over ten thousand years,
unhurried, certain of its inches,
which is the only certainty the river knows
and the only kind that lasts.
We are not the river. We are the weather
on the river — the sudden dark,
the brief bright weather, the fish that leap
once, and are caught mid-air,
and everyone agrees that was the frame.

V.

Keep a list of the small mercies:
the streetlamp that comes on as you pass,
the word that arrives when the sentence is stalling,
the dog that finds you before you find the door,
the song that knows you before the chorus does.
The list is not hope. The list is evidence,
and evidence, kept faithfully,
becomes a kind of light
you can turn to in a dark room.

VI.

The garden does not apologize for its weeds.
It is not a failure if the roses
lean the way the wind leans,
if the pear tree gives its pears
in no order the calendar promised.
The garden is a negotiation
between what was planted and what was not,
and the truce between them
is the whole point of the place.

VII.

At the end of the long road,
the cartographer folds up the map
and looks up from it,
and there is the country,
unmapped, unmeasured,
still being drawn by everyone
who walks it —
and the ink is not dry,
and it never will be,
and that, the blank and the line and the light on the page,
is all the way home.

---
